title: GPU runtime profiling: TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM + CUDA graphs deep dive
next_steps: Redwood to share raw nsys and trace captures + annotated kernel map (Samir)
Customer to run their 8k-context benchmark and share loadgen config (Jason)
Schedule follow-up run with Dedicated cluster to test persistent KV cache (w/ Rina, Marco)
action_items: Samir: upload nsys traces and annotated kernel selection spreadsheet by 2025-06-27
Jason: export and share Novacore 8k loadgen config and sample prompts by 2025-06-29
Rina: prepare test config for persistent KV cache on Dedicated for next run by 2025-07-02
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-06-25 15:00 UTC, Duration 60m, Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Rina Cho (Redwood SE), Jason Lee (Novacore), Priya Natarajan (Novacore SRE), Marco Ruiz (Novacore GPU Eng)

[00:00] Samir: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. today rina and i wanted to walk through the profiling we ran comparing TensorRT-LLM and vLLM and show some cuda graph experiments we did on our dedicated infra. objective is to figure out where the kernel selection gap is and whether CUDA graphs + persistent kv cache give you the latency SLO you mentioned last week.

[00:35] Jason: thanks, yeah main constraint for us is p95 < 120ms for 4k context gen at 8 tokens; also we need deterministic tail behavior for streaming. we also have data residency needs on-prem so the VPC/on-prem discussion matters.

[00:52] Rina: quick agenda: 1) profiling methodology and tools (nsys, nvtx markers), 2) kernel selection differences we observed, 3) cuda graphs results, 4) kv cache and batching interplay, 5) quantization tradeoffs, 6) ops for next run.

[01:18] Marco: curious — are you using TF32 or FP16 baseline for these runs? and what quantization toolkit?

[01:25] Rina: baseline is FP16 for both; TensorRT-LLM runs we tried INT8 calibration with TRT-llm's per-channel calibration. for vLLM we tested Q4_0/Q4_K_M style 4-bit quantizations via GPTQ tools; caveat different toolchains mean kernel mapping differs.

[02:03] Samir: reminder, the goal is practical: not just single-token algo peaks but real request shapes — 50% short prompts, 30% 512 tokens, 20% long 4k contexts. we instrumented with nvtx ranges at token emit, kv read/write, attention kern, softmax.

[02:35] Jason: can you share the raw traces after the call?

[02:38] Rina: yes we will — link to artifacts: short deck + spreadsheet + nsys capture: https://redwood-internal/benchmarks/novacore-tensorrt-vllm.xlsx and nsys tar link: https://redwood-internal/traces/ff-7842-nsys.tar.gz

[03:05] Rina: diving in — first observation: TensorRT-LLM had fewer kernel launches for fused attention + rotary ops because TRT fused a handful of elementwise kernels; vLLM's stack has more small kernels but better dynamic batching at the request layer. result: TRT wins on single-request latency for FP16/INT8 but vLLM achieves higher sustained throughput under high qps due to batching.

[03:38] Jason: that maps to what we suspected. we mainly care about p95 at small qps though — lots of interactive widgets.

[03:45] Rina: right, and we saw that CUDA graphs reduced launch overhead by ~15-25% on average for the TRT flows — particularly when the sequence-length profile is stable and you can pre-build graphs per (seq_len, batch_size) pair. vLLM benefits less from cuda graphs unless you also coalesce the mini-batches into fixed shapes.

[04:15] Priya: slight nit: our on-prem infra disallows persistent root privileges for graph pre-compilation step — how did you do graph snapshotting?

[04:25] Rina: for the Dedicated tests we pre-warmed graphs in a privileged build phase in a controlled container, stored compiled cuda graph objects on a shared volume that the runtime could mmap. if on-prem policy forbids that step we fallback to runtime capture at first request but that adds ~30-40ms spike.

[04:52] Marco: what about kv cache placement — do you keep full kv on GPU memory or host pinned memory?

[04:58] Rina: experiment set A kept KV entirely in GPU DRAM, set B used sharded KV across two GPUs with an async prefetch to local GPU when accessed. full-GPU KV gives best tail latency but increases memory pressure and prevents larger batch sizes; sharded/prefetch reduces memory but adds cross-GPU comms — which showed up as NCCL kernel overhead in traces. we added nvtx markers: you can see the NCCL AllGather spikes at token 1 for long sequences.

[05:40] Samir: note — we saw KV 'cache miss' patterns when context windows jump (e.g., moving from 512->4096) and the runtime had to reallocate. that reallocation showed a 40-80ms penalty in our traces.

[06:00] Jason: any tips to avoid that reallocation on Novacore? we run mixed workloads.

[06:07] Rina: options: 1) reserve worst-case KV memory at session start (higher footprint), 2) use on-demand growth but keep a small pool of pre-allocated chunks to handle expansions, 3) use a persistent KV service (Redwood Dedicated) that pins persistent KV on local SSD+GPU mapping — reduces reallocation cost but requires additional infra config.

[06:35] Marco: about kernel selection — more detail please.

[06:38] Rina: sure. we captured per-kernel name, SM utilization, memory throughput. TRT-LLM tends to pick optimized fused attention kernels (trt_attn_fused) that reduce global mem loads; these kernels have higher occupancy but larger shared memory usage. vLLM's default attention (flash_attn variants) uses more fine-grained tiling with fewer shared mem constraints and is robust across seq lengths. on A100s, trt fused kernels had 10-15% better latency for 1-4 token emits, but when sequence grows the memory-bandwidth-bound kernels in trt degrade slightly.

[07:25] Priya: did you see any non-deterministic behavior from TRT int8 path? we had reproducibility concerns in prod audits.

[07:33] Rina: good call — the INT8 calibration in TRT introduced small output diffs vs FP16 which is expected — we flagged those in the spreadsheet. if you need bit-for-bit reproducibility, stick to FP16 or deterministic int8 configs (at cost to perf). we noted quantization caused occasional tokenization edge shifts in ~0.1% of prompts.

[08:05] Jason: can Redwood run a diff/regression test on our eval set to quantify quality drop?

[08:10] Samir: yes — we'll run the eval harness on your sample set and include Rouge/BLEU/LLM-specific QA checks. will attach results to the traces.

[08:22] Rina: another item: kernel launch overhead — vLLM's many small kernels cause higher launch overhead; CUDA graphs mitigated that but required stable shape. For dynamically shaped requests we recommended a hybrid: small-shape fast-path (prebuilt graph) + general path with a micro-batching scheduler.

[08:50] Marco: micro-batching scheduler — is that Redwood's scheduler or vLLM's?

[08:55] Rina: Redwood runtime includes a continuous-batching layer that coalesces in-flight requests into micro-batches within a tight window (configurable ms). vLLM offers its own batching but it's at a different layer — sometimes you can get both to cooperate but you need to tune thresholds to avoid added latency.

[09:18] Jason: how did you measure tail p95/p99? which load generator?

[09:23] Rina: used a modified loadgen based on wrkload + custom request patterns. we captured p50/p95/p99 and also token-emission histograms. traces include timestamps aligned to token emission.

[09:40] Priya: storage/encryption questions for on-prem: if we store prebuilt cuda graphs or compiled TRT engines, how do you handle KMS and HSM keys for model encryption?

[09:52] Samir: for private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM. compiled engine blobs can be encrypted at rest with customer keys; at runtime the node has to decrypt into protected memory. we outlined workflows in our security packet — we'll share that doc.

[10:12] Marco: any notes on kernel-level NVLink/NCCL tuning? we saw suboptimal AllReduce patterns in our infra earlier.

[10:20] Rina: in our sharded KV runs, enabling NCCL comms overlap and tuning NCCL_P2P_LEVEL and using GDR for host pinned transfers helped. also ensure affinity: numa pinning + cuda mem advices improved effective bandwidth by ~8%. we captured these as env var sets in the spreadsheet.

[10:45] Samir: quick pause — want to show a playback from an nsys capture to highlight a trace region. (shared screen) here at 00:12:40 of the trace you can see the big kernel spike when the context expands; nvtx range shows "kv_realloc" and then multiple cudaMemAlloc calls. that map corresponds to the 65ms spike.

[11:15] Jason: ugh, that matches our production incidents last month.

[11:20] Rina: mitigations: pre-reserve, or add a preflight where the client requests allocation hints before a long context call, or use streaming windows so you avoid a single giant allocate.

[11:40] Priya: would Redwood's Dedicated support pinned persistent KV across requests even if the client disconnects?

[11:48] Samir: yes, Dedicated has session affinity and can retain KV for a configurable TTL; that reduces cold-start. there are tradeoffs on memory billing and eviction policies which we can tune.

[12:05] Marco: about model conversion — did you convert our FP16 checkpoints to TRT engine or rely on on-the-fly building?

[12:12] Rina: we tried both. preconverted TRT engines gave fastest cold start once loaded, but require rebuilds for model tweaks. on-the-fly building is slower but more flexible. we recommend build pipelines in CI to produce validated engine blobs for each release.

[12:35] Jason: what's the recommended quant config if we want to keep p95 under 120ms and limit quality drift?

[12:42] Rina: based on our eval, FP16 + selective int8 on FFN layers (hybrid quant) gave best tradeoff — roughly 1.2-1.8x speedup vs FP16 alone on some layers with <0.5% eval metric delta. full int8 gave more perf but larger quality delta. also consider Q4_K_M for apps tolerant to slight distribution shifts.

[13:10] Priya: any safety nets for unexpected int8 regressions in prod?

[13:15] Samir: automatic rollback policies and dual-write canary: run FP16 and quantized in parallel for a small fraction of traffic and compare scores; Redwood's rollout supports that.

[13:33] Marco: curious about memory pointers: did you see fragmentation from repeated cudaMalloc/free?

[13:38] Rina: yes, frequent malloc/free patterns introduced fragmentation; solution: use a memory pool allocator or bump allocator with periodic GC during low traffic. also recommended avoiding per-request cudaMalloc.

[13:56] Jason: are there recommendations for node sizing for our traffic shape? we have many small interactions but occasional long sessions.

[14:03] Rina: for mixed workloads we suggested medium-sized nodes with high GPU memory (A100 80GB type) and to enable session affinity + persistent KV TTL. autoscale with burst capacity so long sessions don't starve small request latency.

[14:25] Samir: wrapping up with a concrete plan: we'll share traces + annotated kernel map; Redwood will run customer's eval set across TRT-int8, TRT-FP16, vLLM-FP16, vLLM-Q4 variants and return a table mapping p50/p95/p99, throughput, and quality metrics. then we'll run a Dedicated pilot with persistent KV graph prewarm to validate tail behavior.

[14:50] Jason: sounds good. timeline?

[14:53] Samir: we'll push artifacts by Friday (2025-06-27), customer runs sample eval by end of next week. follow-up meeting in 2 weeks.

[15:00] Priya: any compliance docs we should expect for Dedicated/on-prem?

[15:04] Samir: yes — SOC2/ISO packet, KMS integration notes, and our on-prem install checklist. will attach.

[15:15] Marco: small note — in one trace i think a kernel name got truncated in the nsys output as "trt_attn_fu..." — hope that's not an issue.

[15:22] Rina: that happens with long kernel names in the UI; we'll include raw name mapping in the spreadsheet.

[15:32] Samir: ok final recap: action items and next steps as above, we'll schedule the Dedicated pilot run and set up a shared folder for artifacts. thanks folks.

[15:45] Jason: thanks all, very helpful.

[15:48] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker attribution errors and truncation in kernel names; some filler words omitted.
summary: Deep technical profiling comparing TensorRT-LLM and vLLM on Redwood infra. Key findings: TRT fused kernels give lower single-request latency (FP16/INT8), vLLM offers better sustained throughput via dynamic batching. CUDA graphs reduce kernel launch overhead especially for stable shapes. KV cache placement strongly affects tail latency; pre-reserving or persistent KV on Dedicated reduces large reallocation spikes. Quantization tradeoffs: hybrid selective int8 beneficial; full int8 causes minor quality regressions. On-prem constraints (KMS, graph prebuild privileges) and NCCL tuning discussed. Next steps: share traces, run customer eval, schedule Dedicated pilot.
